interest: This file provides valuable historical insight into the gradual evolution and enforcement of child labor and social welfare legislation in interwar Japan between 1923 and 1933. It documents Japan's efforts to modernize industrial labor standards in the wake of the 1919 ILO Washington Conference through the 1923 Factory Law amendments, while highlighting the political compromises made, such as multi-year transition periods and exemptions for agriculture and small commerce. Furthermore, Consul General Garrels's 1933 report preserves rare quantitative municipal sociological data on vulnerable urban youth in Tokyo, enumerating child street peddlers, beggars, singers, and child geishas, while illustrating the practical dilemma of providing state relief to impoverished families dependent on juvenile earnings.
overview: This file (decimal 894.5047) covers U.S. State Department diplomatic and consular reporting from Tokyo between May 1923 and October 1933 regarding child labor and protective social legislation in Japan. The materials include a May 1923 despatch from Chargé d'Affaires Hugh R. Wilson enclosing an English translation of Law No. 23 (the 1923 amendments to the Factory Law of 1911), which raised the minimum employment age, limited hours for women and juvenile workers under sixteen, and placed restrictions on hazardous and night labor. The file concludes with an October 1933 consular report by Consul General Arthur Garrels on the enactment of the Child Welfare Law, which prohibited the exploitation of children under fourteen in begging, peddling, entertainment, and serving in drinking establishments, accompanied by statistics on affected children in Tokyo and government relief efforts for impoverished families.

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note indicating that Despatch No. 594 from Japan regarding the amended Factory Law was filed under decimal file 894.5041/1.
subfiles.summary: A Department of State Document File Note recording Despatch No. 594 sent from Tokyo by Chargé d'Affaires Hugh R. Wilson on May 12, 1923. It directs researchers to decimal file 894.5041/1 for the original despatch. The note summarizes that the despatch encloses a translation of the Factory Law amended by the Imperial Diet prohibiting the employment of minors under 15 years of age.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Despatch No. 594

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting a translation of the amended Japanese Factory Law and explaining new statutory restrictions on child labor in industrial sectors.
subfiles.summary: U.S. Chargé d'Affaires a.i. Hugh R. Wilson reports to the Secretary of State on the passage and official promulgation of amendments to the Japanese Factory Law alongside supplementary legislation. The enacted measures prohibit the employment of minors under fifteen in factories, mines, quarries, dockyards, construction, and building trades, with an exemption for minors over twelve who have finished primary school. Wilson transmits an English translation of the amended statute for the Department's records.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 594 from Hugh R. Wilson on the Amended Factory Law

subfiles.about: Official English translation of Japanese Law No. 23 amending the Factory Law of 1911 regarding working hours, child labor, and workplace safety.
subfiles.summary: An official translation of Law No. 23 sanctioned on March 29, 1923, which extensively revised Japan's 1911 Factory Law. The statute restricts working hours for women and male minors under sixteen to eleven hours per day, mandates rest periods and bimonthly holidays, and prohibits night work between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. It further bans minors and female workers from cleaning or repairing machinery in motion and handling toxic or explosive substances, establishes employer liability for industrial injuries and deaths, and outlines administrative inspection and penalty procedures.
subfiles.title: Translation of Law No. 23: Law Amending the Factory Law

subfiles.about: Consular report detailing the provisions and initial enforcement of Japan's new Child Welfare Law protecting minors under fourteen from exploitation.
subfiles.summary: American Consul General Arthur Garrels reports on the entry into force of Japan's Child Welfare Law on October 1, 1933, characterizing it as a landmark social policy development. The statute prohibits the employment of children under fourteen as beggars, street peddlers, acrobats, or as waitresses and geishas in establishments serving sake, while penalizing the public commercial display of crippled children. Drawing on data from Tokyo's Municipal Children's Bureau, Garrels notes that over 1,500 children in Tokyo were affected, summarizes family relief programs for lost wages, and reviews earlier child labor prohibitions in manufacturing and maritime work.
subfiles.title: Report on Child Welfare Law by Arthur Garrels
